turns.speaker: Pip
turns.text: Yes, Miss Havisham.

turns.speaker: Miss Havisham
turns.text: Estella, show this boy the house and let him see what you see.

turns.speaker: Pip
turns.text: Yes, Miss Havisham. I'll be glad to see the house.

turns.speaker: Miss Havisham
turns.text: Take him to the rooms I showed you yesterday, Estella. Let him see the clocks.

turns.speaker: Pip
turns.text: Yes, Miss Havisham. I will follow Estella to see the rooms.

turns.speaker: Miss Havisham
turns.text: Very well, Pip. Your curiosity will amuse me.

turns.speaker: Pip
turns.text: Yes, Miss Havisham. I'll go with Estella now.

turns.speaker: Miss Havisham
turns.text: Remember, Pip, the rooms hold memories of a different time. Observe them well, but do not touch.

turns.speaker: Pip
turns.text: Yes, Miss Havisham. I'll be careful.

turns.speaker: Miss Havisham
turns.text: Watch Estella closely, Pip. There are lessons to be learned from her composure.

turns.speaker: Pip
turns.text: Yes, Miss Havisham. I will pay attention to Estella.

turns.speaker: Miss Havisham
turns.text: Pip, you remind me of someone from long ago. Observe and learn, for there is much to discern in the world.

turns.speaker: Pip
turns.text: Thank you, Miss Havisham. I will try my best to understand everything here.

turns.speaker: Miss Havisham
turns.text: Ah, Pip, the world is a complex tapestry of joys and sorrows. Remember that.

turns.speaker: Pip
turns.text: Yes, Miss Havisham. I see that the world can be both joyful and sad, like the place you live in.

turns.speaker: Miss Havisham
turns.text: Ah, Pip, the world is indeed a place of contrasts. But remember, it is the bitterness that teaches us the most.

turns.speaker: Pip
turns.text: I understand, Miss Havisham. I see the sadness in this place, but I also see the beauty of the old things around us.

turns.speaker: Miss Havisham
turns.text: Yes, Pip, the beauty in the decay is a lesson in itself. Can you see through the rust and dust?

turns.speaker: Pip
turns.text: Miss Havisham, I can see the beauty, but I also feel the sadness. It's like the old things are holding onto something they've lost.

turns.speaker: Miss Havisham
turns.text: Ah, Pip, you are wise beyond your years. The beauty here is a reflection of what once was, and the sadness, my dear, is the shadow of what could have been.

opening.speaker: Pip
opening.text: Mr. Pumblechook’s boy, ma’am. Come—to play.

opening.speaker: Miss Havisham
opening.text: Come nearer; let me look at you. Come close.

opening.speaker: Miss Havisham
opening.text: Look at me. You are not afraid of a woman who has never seen the sun since you were born?

opening.speaker: Miss Havisham
opening.text: Do you know what I touch here?

opening.speaker: Miss Havisham
opening.text: I am tired. I want diversion, and I have done with men and women. Play.

opening.speaker: Miss Havisham
opening.text: I sometimes have sick fancies, and I have a sick fancy that I want to see some play. There, there! with an impatient movement of the fingers of her right hand; play, play, play!

opening.speaker: Pip
opening.text: No, ma’am, I am very sorry for you, and very sorry I can’t play just now. If you complain of me I shall get into trouble with my sister, so I would do it if I could; but it’s so new here, and so strange, and so fine,—and melancholy—.

opening.speaker: Miss Havisham
opening.text: So new to him, so old to me; so strange to him, so familiar to me; so melancholy to both of us! Call Estella.
